questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of earthing mains-powered equipment in the amateur shack?
options: To prevent radio frequency interference from reaching neighbouring properties
To provide a low-resistance path so that fault current flows to earth rather than through the operator, causing the fuse or breaker to trip
To reduce the noise floor of the receiver by draining static charges from the antenna
To meet Ofcom's requirement for a station earth as a condition of the Full licence
questions.explanation: Earthing provides a deliberate low-resistance path to earth for fault current. If the mains live conductor contacts the equipment chassis, current takes the earth path rather than the path through the operator, and the resulting high current blows the fuse or trips the circuit breaker. Without a proper earth, a faulty chassis may remain at mains potential and a person touching it provides the only path to earth — with potentially fatal consequences.

questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: An indicator lamp on your linear amplifier's HT supply is not illuminated. What should you conclude before touching internal components?
options: The supply is de-energised and it is safe to proceed without further checks
The lamp is not lit, so the HT supply has definitely been discharged by the bleed resistors
A lamp that is not lit does not confirm the supply is safe — the lamp itself may have failed; always verify with a meter before touching anything
The equipment has entered standby mode and the HT is reduced to a safe level automatically
questions.explanation: Indicator lamps are a useful reminder that a circuit is live, but a lamp that is not lit does not mean the equipment is safe. The lamp itself can fail while the dangerous voltage remains present. Before touching any internal component — especially in equipment with high-voltage supplies such as valve rigs and linear amplifiers — always use a suitably rated meter to confirm the voltage is absent.

questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: You need to replace a component on a circuit board inside a mains-powered transceiver. Which procedure correctly applies the Full licence safety guidance?
options: Switch the transceiver off at the front panel, leave it plugged in, and allow 30 seconds for capacitors to discharge
Work with the power on so you can test the circuit as you replace the component
Switch the transceiver off AND unplug the mains lead before replacing any component or circuit board
Switch the transceiver to receive-only mode, which reduces the internal voltages to a safer level
questions.explanation: For the replacement of circuit boards or components, the correct procedure is to turn the equipment off AND unplug it from the mains. Switching off at the front panel without unplugging leaves mains voltage present at the power supply input and does not guarantee that internal capacitors have discharged. Unplugging removes the energy source and is the only certain way to ensure the equipment is de-energised before work begins.

questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: What key difference distinguishes an RCBO from a standard RCD?
options: An RCBO trips in 10 ms whereas an RCD takes 25–40 ms, making it faster in a fault
An RCBO combines earth-fault detection with overcurrent protection in a single unit, whereas an RCD detects earth faults only
An RCD is rated for outdoor use and an RCBO is for indoor installations only
An RCBO requires a separate earth rod while an RCD uses the property mains earth
questions.explanation: An RCD (Residual Current Device) detects current imbalance between live and neutral — indicating an earth fault — and disconnects the circuit. It does not provide protection against overload or short circuit. An RCBO (Residual Current Circuit Breaker with Overcurrent protection) combines both functions in one unit: it acts as an RCD for earth faults and as a circuit breaker for overcurrent. For full circuit-level protection, an RCBO is the preferred device.

questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: The standard trip threshold for a 30 mA RCD is 25–40 ms. Why does this threshold matter in the context of electrocution risk?
options: The 30 mA threshold is chosen to prevent nuisance tripping from normal equipment leakage, with no direct link to physiological harm
A current of less than 100 mA can stop the heart; the 30 mA trip provides a safety margin below this level, disconnecting the circuit before a potentially fatal current builds up
30 mA is the maximum current that any mains circuit breaker can safely interrupt without arcing
At currents above 30 mA, damage to wiring insulation begins to occur, so the RCD protects the cable rather than the person
questions.explanation: Physiological research shows that a current of less than 100 mA is sufficient to cause ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. The standard 30 mA RCD threshold provides a significant safety margin below this level, and the 25–40 ms trip time ensures disconnection well before the current can accumulate enough energy to cause irreversible cardiac effects. The 30 mA threshold is specifically a people-protection standard, not a cable-protection standard.

questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: You are taking a voltage measurement inside a linear amplifier running at 2 kV HT with the power on. Which precaution specifically reduces the risk of current passing through your chest cavity?
options: Stand on an insulating rubber mat to increase the resistance of the path to ground
Use a meter with a 10 MΩ input impedance to limit the current through the probe
Keep one hand in your pocket or behind your back so that both hands cannot simultaneously contact the circuit
Wear insulating gloves rated to at least 5 kV before making any measurement
questions.explanation: The one-hand rule — keeping one hand in a pocket or behind your back while probing with the other — eliminates the most dangerous current path, which runs from hand to hand through the chest and across the heart. If only one hand is in contact with the circuit, any current must find an alternative path to earth (typically via the feet), which, while still hazardous, is less likely to cause cardiac arrest than a hand-to-heart-to-hand path.

questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: Why should headphones not be worn when adjusting live high-voltage equipment in the shack?
options: Headphone cables act as antennas and can conduct RF into the head, increasing radiation exposure
An unexpected burst of audio — such as a relay closing or a signal appearing — can cause an involuntary flinching movement at exactly the moment when hand control is most critical
Headphones insulate the ears from ambient warning sounds such as burning smells or relay clicks
The headphone impedance bridges the test probe return path, giving false meter readings
questions.explanation: Wearing headphones when working on live equipment is specifically discouraged because a sudden unexpected sound — a relay closing, a strong signal arriving, feedback — can cause an involuntary startle or flinch. Near high-voltage circuitry, any sudden uncontrolled movement of the hands carries serious risk of contact with a lethal voltage. Removing headphones eliminates this involuntary-response hazard while working inside live equipment.

questions.section_name: Safe Use of Electricity in the Shack
questions.question: You are about to measure a resistance on a component inside a piece of shack equipment. The equipment is switched off but still plugged into the mains. Applying all relevant safety principles, what is the correct approach?
options: A resistance measurement uses only a small current from the meter battery, so plugged-in equipment poses no additional risk; proceed with the measurement
Unplug the mains lead, wait for internal capacitors to discharge, then take the resistance measurement with one hand in your pocket in case residual charge remains
Switch the equipment off at the front panel before measuring, as the mains does not reach the component level unless the equipment is switched on
The measurement requires the equipment to be powered for the reading to be meaningful, so switch on and proceed carefully
questions.explanation: Resistance measurements must always be made with power removed and with the circuit fully discharged. Switching off at the front panel is insufficient — mains voltage is still present at the power supply input, and large filter capacitors in the supply can retain charge at lethal voltages for several minutes after switch-off. Unplugging removes the energy source; waiting for capacitors to discharge (or checking with a high-voltage meter) before probing is essential. The one-hand precaution is still appropriate if any residual charge is suspected.

questions.section_name: Safety at Temporary Locations and Public Events
questions.question: Before erecting a temporary antenna mast at a public event, what site survey check is specifically required regarding overhead infrastructure?
options: Confirm that there are no trees within 5 metres of the intended mast position
Verify that the ground is firm enough to support the mast base without a concrete footing
Identify any overhead power lines and ensure the mast cannot touch them even if it falls in any direction
Check that the site has an existing mains earth rod at least 1 metre deep
questions.explanation: A key requirement of the site survey before erecting any vertical antenna or mast is to identify overhead power lines. The mast must be positioned far enough away that even if it falls over — in any direction — it cannot reach and contact the power lines. This accounts for the full height of the structure and the direction of any likely fall. Contact between an antenna structure and power lines would be potentially fatal to anyone nearby.

questions.section_name: Safety at Temporary Locations and Public Events
questions.question: Mains cables are being run across a public walkway at a Special Event Station. Which is the correct way to manage this hazard?
options: Tape the cable flat to the ground with gaffer tape at 50 cm intervals along its length
Route the cable under rubber cable protectors designed for walkway use, so the cable is covered and trip-free
Suspend the cable at head height using cable ties to nearby structures so it is out of foot traffic
Mark the cable's path with cones on either side to warn pedestrians of the hazard
questions.explanation: Where cables must cross a pedestrian walkway, rubber cable protectors — ramp-style covers designed for this purpose — are the correct solution. These covers hold the cable flat against the floor, create a smooth ramp over which pedestrians and wheelchair users can pass, and are clearly visible. Gaffer tape alone leaves a raised edge that is still a trip hazard. Cones warn of a hazard but do not eliminate it.

questions.section_name: Safety at Temporary Locations and Public Events
questions.question: You are running a Special Event Station using a petrol generator. During the event a fire starts in the generator area. Which fire extinguisher type is appropriate, and why is water not suitable?
options: A water extinguisher — it is the most effective for rapid cooling and is safe to use near electrical equipment
A CO₂ or dry powder extinguisher — these are suitable for fuel (Class B) and electrical fires; water would spread burning fuel and risk electrocution
A foam extinguisher — foam forms a blanket over the fuel fire and prevents re-ignition
Any extinguisher rated for Class A fires is acceptable because wood and fabric are the primary combustibles in a marquee
questions.explanation: Petrol and diesel are Class B (flammable liquid) fires. Water must never be used on fuel fires: it can cause burning fuel to splash and spread the fire, and can also cause steam explosions. CO₂ extinguishers smother the fire by displacing oxygen without leaving residue; dry powder extinguishers chemically interrupt combustion and are also suitable. Both types are also safe to use near electrical equipment, which is present in any generator installation.

questions.section_name: Safety at Temporary Locations and Public Events
questions.question: When carrying out a formal risk assessment for a Special Event Station, what are the two separate factors that must be assessed for each hazard, and how is an overall risk score derived?
options: The probability of the hazard occurring and the cost of the mitigation required; risk score = probability ÷ cost
The number of people potentially affected and the duration of exposure; risk score = people × hours
The likelihood of the hazard occurring and the severity of harm if it does; risk score = likelihood × severity
The frequency of similar incidents nationally and the number of trained first-aiders on site; risk score = frequency × first-aiders
questions.explanation: A formal risk assessment requires each identified hazard to be rated on two independent axes: how likely it is to occur, and how severe the resulting harm would be if it did occur. Multiplying these two scores gives a numerical risk rating. Higher-rated risks require stronger mitigation measures, which must be documented. Documenting the assessment is essential: if an incident occurs at the event, insurers and investigators will want to see it.

questions.section_name: Safety at Temporary Locations and Public Events
questions.question: At a public Special Event Station you are running 400 W into a vertical antenna at 2 m above ground level. Why must RF exposure be explicitly included in the risk assessment for this event?
options: Ofcom requires all stations above 100 W to file a separate RF exposure report within 48 hours of a public event
At a public event, members of the public may approach much closer to the antenna than would be possible in a domestic shack, so compliance distances must be calculated and enforced
RF exposure is only relevant when operating on VHF and UHF frequencies, not HF
RF exposure in the risk assessment is optional for event stations operating below 1 kW
questions.explanation: In a domestic shack, the antenna is typically elevated and separated from the public by the property boundary. At a public event, a low-mounted antenna can be approached by members of the public — including children — who may walk into the near-field. The compliance distance (exclusion zone) must be calculated, and if it extends into the public area, physical barriers or power reductions are required. RF exposure is therefore a mandatory element of the risk assessment for any public event, regardless of frequency.

questions.section_name: Safety at Temporary Locations and Public Events
questions.question: You are about to connect a 5 A rated piece of equipment to a 13 A fused mains outlet at a portable event. Why does a 13 A fuse provide inadequate protection for this equipment?
options: A 13 A fuse operates too slowly for the sensitive electronics in modern transceivers

The fuse will not blow until the circuit is drawing well above 5 A — at 5 A normal load the fuse provides no overcurrent protection; it will only interrupt at currents far exceeding the equipment's rated maximum
Plug-top fuses are not approved for use outdoors; a separate RCD must be substituted
A 13 A fuse has a higher voltage rating than a 5 A fuse and may cause the supply voltage to increase
questions.explanation: A fuse protects the cable and equipment by blowing when the current exceeds the fuse rating. A 13 A fuse in a 5 A circuit will not blow at 5 A normal operating current — it will only interrupt if the fault current rises well above 13 A. This means a developing fault or overload in a 5 A rated device can draw several amperes above the equipment's design limit for an extended period before the fuse operates, potentially causing insulation damage or fire. Equipment should always be fused as close to its rated current as practicable.

questions.section_name: Safety at Temporary Locations and Public Events
questions.question: You are operating a portable Special Event Station outdoors using mains power from a road-side supply. Shortly after connecting, the RCD trips. You reset it and it trips again immediately. Which sequence of actions is correct?
options: Replace the RCD with a higher-rated model — repeated tripping indicates the trip threshold is set too sensitively for outdoor use
Do not reset the RCD again; systematically disconnect equipment one item at a time, inspect each mains lead and plug for damage, identify the faulty item before reconnecting anything
Switch everything off at the front panel of each item and reset the RCD — repeated tripping is normal in wet weather until the supply stabilises
Bypass the RCD temporarily and use the MCB in the distribution board, which has a higher trip current and will not nuisance-trip
questions.explanation: A repeatedly tripping RCD indicates a real earth-fault condition is present — not a nuisance trip. The correct response is to not attempt further resets until the fault is found. Disconnect all equipment, inspect every mains lead, plug, and connector for signs of damage, moisture ingress, or exposed conductor, and identify the faulty item before reconnecting. Bypassing or replacing the RCD to get around a genuine fault would remove the only protection against an earth fault that could be lethal — particularly outdoors where ground conductivity is high.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: According to FCS 1362 vehicle wiring guidance, how should the negative DC lead from a mobile transceiver be connected?
options: Via a suitably rated fuse directly to the battery negative terminal
To the vehicle chassis via a suitable earth point, without a fuse in the negative lead
To the battery negative terminal via the vehicle's chassis bonding strap and a 30 A fuse
Via the vehicle's existing fuse box to share the negative return with other accessories
questions.explanation: FCS 1362 specifies that the negative lead connects directly to the vehicle chassis (a suitable earth point close to the transceiver), and this lead must not be fused. Fusing the negative return is incorrect because if the negative fuse blows during a fault, the chassis of the transceiver can rise to supply voltage relative to the true vehicle chassis, creating an electric shock and fire risk. The positive lead from the battery must always be fused close to the battery terminal.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: You are operating a vehicle-mounted HF transceiver while driving. Using a hand-held microphone is not the same legal situation as using a handheld mobile phone, but why should you still avoid it?
options: Using a hand-held microphone causes significant RF exposure to the driver's head at HF frequencies
It is prohibited under the current Road Traffic Act in the same way as a handheld mobile phone
It can lead to prosecution for driving without due care and attention and will be significant in any subsequent accident investigation, and may affect motor insurance
It reduces the quality of the audio transmission, making it difficult for the other station to copy your signal
questions.explanation: Using a hand-held microphone while driving is not defined as a prima facie offence equivalent to the handheld mobile phone prohibition, but it diverts attention from driving and risks prosecution for driving without due care and attention. If an accident occurs while using a hand-held microphone, it will be a significant factor in any police investigation and is likely to affect insurance validity. Strongly recommended practice is remote PTT switching and a hands-free boom or headset microphone, with any retuning performed only when stationary.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: What is the only biologically significant effect of RF energy on body tissue, according to the ICNIRP framework adopted in the amateur licence?
options: Ionisation of DNA strands, which is cumulative and increases cancer risk with prolonged exposure
Disruption of ion channels in nerve cell membranes, causing temporary sensory disturbance
Heating of body tissue by RF currents induced in the cells — a risk only when the heat generated exceeds what the body's own temperature regulation can remove
Electromagnetic interference with implanted cardiac devices such as pacemakers and defibrillators
questions.explanation: The ICNIRP framework — referenced in Condition 9-1 of the amateur licence — recognises heating as the only proven biologically significant effect of RF energy at the frequencies and levels relevant to amateur radio. RF currents induced in tissue generate heat. This only becomes a hazard when the thermal load exceeds the body's ability to regulate temperature. RF energy at amateur power levels is non-ionising and cannot break DNA bonds. The ICNIRP limits are set with substantial safety margins to prevent significant tissue heating.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: A static discharge device is fitted in the antenna feeder of your HF station. A thunderstorm is now directly overhead. What action should you take, and why is the discharge device insufficient protection on its own?
options: No action is needed — the discharge device is specifically designed to handle direct lightning strikes, which is why it is fitted
Switch the transceiver to receive-only mode — the discharge device protects the transmitter but not the receiver
Disconnect the feeder from the equipment and move the connector away from the radio; static discharge devices protect against charge build-up but cannot handle the energy of a direct lightning strike
Switch on the transceiver and transmit a carrier — a continuous transmission keeps the feeder at a known potential and prevents charge accumulation
questions.explanation: Static discharge devices present a low-impedance path for slowly accumulating static charge, allowing it to drain to earth safely before it reaches a damaging level. However, they are completely inadequate against the energy of a direct lightning return stroke, which carries megavolts in a fraction of a second. When a storm is directly overhead, the only reliable protection is to disconnect the antenna feeder from the equipment and physically move the RF connector away from the radio. Nothing short of a full BS EN/IEC 62305 installation guards against a direct strike.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: You install an RF earth (copper rod in the garden) for your HF station. Your property has a PME (TN-C-S) mains supply. What must you do before this RF earth can safely be used?
options: Nothing additional is required — a copper earth rod simply improves the ground plane for the antenna and poses no safety concern
Bond the RF earth to the property's Main Earth Terminal (MET) using a substantial conductor, inspected by a qualified electrician, as the work is notifiable under Part P
Ensure the RF earth rod is at least 2 metres deep and at least 5 metres from the house foundations, after which it can be connected directly to the transceiver chassis
Install an isolating transformer between the mains supply and all shack equipment, which separates the mains earth from the RF earth without bonding
questions.explanation: In a PME system, the mains earth is bonded to the neutral at the Main Earth Terminal, forming an equipotential zone. An independent RF earth rod is at soil potential, which differs from the PME earth potential. Any equipment connected to both earths — such as a transceiver with a mains earth via its power supply and an RF earth via its antenna connector — bridges this potential difference, creating a shock risk. The mandatory solution is to bond the RF earth to the MET, bringing it into the same equipotential zone. This bonding is notifiable work under Part P of the Building Regulations (England and Wales) and must be carried out and inspected by a qualified electrician.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: A storm is approaching your home station. You have a commercial inert-gas static discharge device fitted in the antenna feedline. You are away from home and cannot disconnect the antenna manually. Which statement best describes your level of protection?
options: You are fully protected — the commercial gas-discharge device is specifically rated to handle direct lightning strikes and will conduct the return stroke safely to earth

You are protected against static charge build-up, which may prevent some types of equipment damage from the pre-storm static precursor, but you are not protected against the energy of a direct lightning strike
You have no protection at all — discharge devices only work when the operator is physically present to monitor them
You are protected against equipment damage but not against fire, since discharge devices route current through the antenna mast rather than to earth
questions.explanation: Commercial static discharge devices — whether inert-gas filled or spark-plug type — work by providing a low-impedance path to earth for slowly accumulating static charge, preventing it from building to a level that would damage receiver input stages. This protection is real and useful, and it operates automatically without the operator being present. However, the energy in a direct lightning return stroke is many orders of magnitude greater than these devices can handle. They will not protect against a direct strike. Physical disconnection by an operator present at the station remains the only reliable method of protecting against a nearby or direct strike.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: Your property has a PME mains supply. The neutral conductor fails in the street cabling. Your RF earth is NOT bonded to the MET. Working through the sequence of events, what is the most serious immediate hazard in your shack?
options: The mains live conductor rises to 460 V as the supply becomes unbalanced, potentially overloading all connected equipment

The RF earth may carry return current from the whole house, and the potential difference between the mains earth (which has risen toward 230 V relative to true earth) and the RF earth means that simultaneously touching a mains-connected item and your RF-earth-connected transceiver could be fatal
The RCD immediately trips on neutral loss, so all shack equipment is de-energised within 40 ms and there is no hazard
The transceiver's antenna connector, connected to the RF earth, may develop an RF feedback path that causes spurious emissions on all connected bands
questions.explanation: When the neutral fails upstream of the property in a PME system, return current from all connected appliances needs a path back to the substation. With an unbonded RF earth present, current may flow via the RF earth rod through the soil to DNO earth points — potentially overheating the RF earth conductor. More critically, the house mains earth and neutral (bonded at the MET) may rise toward 230 V relative to true (soil) earth. The RF earth rod remains at true soil potential. A person simultaneously touching a mains-connected item (at 230 V relative to soil) and the transceiver chassis (connected to the RF earth, at soil potential) faces a 230 V potential difference — a potentially fatal shock. This is exactly why bonding the RF earth to the MET is mandatory.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: Your RF earth is correctly bonded to the MET in your PME-supplied property. The neutral fails in the street AND the RF earth bonding cable then also fails (corrodes through). What is the consequence for the rest of the property — not just the shack?
options: Only the shack is affected; the rest of the property is protected by the MET bonding of central heating pipes and water services
The RCD in the shack consumer unit trips, isolating the shack from the rest of the property and limiting the fault to the shack circuit

The entire house earth and neutral rise toward 230 V relative to true earth; all mains-connected equipment with a metal chassis throughout the property becomes live at 230 V relative to ground — the hazard extends to every room
The fault causes the supply transformer to trip, removing power from all properties on the same street supply
questions.explanation: In a PME system, the house mains earth and neutral are bonded together at the MET. If the neutral fails in the street and the RF earth bonding cable also fails, the entire PME earth — which is bonded to all exposed metalwork throughout the property via the supplementary bonding — can rise to 230 V relative to true earth. This is not limited to the shack: every mains-connected appliance with a metal chassis, every bonded water pipe, every radiator, becomes live at 230 V relative to true ground. Anyone touching a mains-connected item and a true-earth reference (soil, plastic-piped water source, etc.) simultaneously faces a potentially fatal shock anywhere in the property. This is why the bonding cable must be of adequate cross-section and inspected periodically.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: All services entering your property (water and gas) use plastic pipes. You want to install an RF earth and are wondering whether the PME bonding requirements apply to you. Which statement is correct?
options: Plastic pipes mean PME bonding is never required — there are no metal services to create a hazard, so the RF earth can be connected directly to the transceiver

The plastic service entries mean the internal metalwork (pipes, radiators) is not connected to the soil via the service entry and is effectively floating; however, if any service enters via a metal pipe, a qualified electrician must assess whether MET bonding is required — and you should consult an electrician regardless
Plastic pipes are irrelevant to PME bonding; what matters is the age of the property, not the material of the service pipes
Plastic pipes mean the equipotential bonding inside the property fails completely, making PME unsafe; you must apply to your DNO for a TN-S supply instead
questions.explanation: Where all services enter a property via plastic pipes, the internal metal pipework (radiators, taps, central heating) is not connected to the soil through the service entry, so it floats with the house equipotential zone rather than providing an alternative path to true earth. In this specific case, Building Regulations may not require bonding of the RF earth to the MET. However, the condition 'all services via plastic' must be verified: if any single service enters via a metal pipe, the equipotential zone is affected and bonding may still be required. The assessment must be made by a qualified electrician — not by the amateur.

questions.section_name: Vehicle Safety, RF Exposure, Thunderstorms and PME
questions.question: You are installing a 100 W transceiver in your car. The RF power amplifier module will be mounted in the boot. What wiring precautions are required to avoid interference with the vehicle's ECU and safety systems?
options: The PA module cables must be routed through the vehicle fuse box to limit the current that can reach sensitive circuits

RF transmitter and PA cables must be kept well away from the vehicle wiring loom and electronic control units, the installation must comply with any manufacturer recommendations on power level and antenna location, and the equipment should be specified as suitable for in-vehicle use
Screen all PA cables in earthed copper braid and route them parallel to the vehicle chassis to maximise shielding effectiveness
Fit a 30 mA RCD in the DC supply to the PA to prevent RF currents reaching the ECU via the battery return path
questions.explanation: Modern vehicles contain numerous safety-critical ECUs — engine management, ABS, airbag deployment, stability control. RF interference with these systems is a genuine safety hazard, not merely an inconvenience. The required precautions are: route RF-carrying cables and the PA unit well away from the vehicle wiring loom and all ECU modules; comply with any manufacturer limits on RF power level and antenna positioning for in-vehicle installations; and use equipment specified and tested for vehicular use. Failure to observe these precautions may also invalidate the vehicle's roadworthiness and the driver's insurance.
